label: profitability and feasibility
overview: Profit and cost pressure scenarios cover two distinct but connected situations: clients struggling with margin squeeze, rising costs, or declining profitability; and clients seeking to fund or acquire assets and needing feasibility assessment before committing. In both cases the advisor's role is to introduce objective, data-driven tools that quantify the problem and demonstrate what improvement is genuinely possible. The four materials below are the rationale for using a revenue model at all, the feasibility framework for testing a purchase, and the two methods for putting a model in front of a client — Cautious Reveal where awareness is low, Trial Fit where it is already high.

materials.name: Why Use Revenue Models
materials.summary: Explains what a revenue model does for the advisor: it shifts the burden of proof away from personal credibility and onto objective, data-driven scenarios. That matters most for newer or younger advisors, who otherwise have only their own experience to prove they can make a difference. It also prices the work, because the fee follows the financial improvement the model identifies.
materials.who_when: Any advisor introducing the revenue model concept to a client — at the start of the advisory relationship, or when recommending a modelling tool inside a profit improvement conversation.
steps: Use the model in the first meeting to check you and the owner understand the business the same way — ask for their feedback and modify rows or columns to fit their specific reality.
Define the business variables in the model clearly, so their effects are quantified rather than asserted.
Adjust the variables in front of them — tweak the margin, add a few extra customers, improve turnaround times — and let them watch the financial impact move.
Put a number on the opportunity: seeing $70,000 to $90,000 of potential growth builds belief in a way a verbal pitch cannot.
Frame the projection without overpromising: "I'm not saying it'll be easy, just suggesting the numbers say it's possible."
Price the advisory service against the projected improvement the model has identified.

materials.name: Lite Feasibility Framework
materials.summary: A three-phase conversational tool for testing whether a proposed loan, funding request or asset purchase actually pays back: understanding the why, proving the how, then preparing for the worst. By the time a client asks for help securing funding they usually carry confirmation bias — they have decided they want the asset and are focused on getting the money. The advisor's job here is devil's advocate: test the idea objectively, or show that the capital would work harder somewhere else.
materials.who_when: Clients seeking funding, a loan or an asset purchase — particularly where the advisor can sense the decision has already been made emotionally.
steps: The Situation — ask first whether there is existing demand for the product or service the asset will support. If the concept is new, the client will have to educate the market.
Where education is required, verify they have both a marketing budget and the financial reserves to survive the time market acceptance takes.
Have the client write down the specific problems or frustrations this purchase will solve — in writing, so minor annoyances separate from real financial barriers.
Ask them to rate on a scale of 1 to 10 how solving each problem impacts revenue or profit; an asset can fix an irritation without improving the bottom line.
Gauge the market size and the financial upside, then challenge it: could this money be invested in a different area of the business for a bigger payback?
The Business Model — ask directly, "show me the money", and document exactly how the funding or asset will contribute to revenue or profit.
Calculate break-even as a utilisation rate: exactly how many times the asset needs to spin around to pay for itself.
The Acid Test — establish what is genuinely at risk if it fails. Would it be an inconvenience, or the straw that breaks the camel's back and pulls the whole business under?
Establish the ripcord: how the client will identify the early signs of failure, and how quickly they can get out.

Where the exit strategy is selling the asset, warn them about market correlation — if their business slows because the market dropped, everyone else is offloading the same asset at the same time, and the realisation rate falls with it.

materials.name: Cautious Reveal Method
materials.summary: A layered way of introducing a revenue model to a client whose awareness or motivation is low, establishing why they need one before they ever see the numbers. It exists to prevent map shock — the overwhelm of meeting a complex model in one hit, which pushes a client straight into judgement, embarrassment and rejection. The reveal ends deliberately unfinished, with a gap of time before the client sees a model of their own.
materials.who_when: Clients with little awareness of revenue models — a standard end-of-year meeting is the typical setting. Used before the Trial Fit method, not instead of it.
steps: Warm the client up beforehand where you can: the "Phil's a plumber" video works as email outreach or inside an introductory quiz, and frames the value before any numbers appear. Find it under Get the Job, search "video", then Video Hyperlinks.
Anchor the concept first — "Have you heard the term overtrading before?" — and use visual aids to explain the profit sweet spot and the risk of growing too fast on debt without guaranteed demand.
Tell the story in a completely different industry, such as a cafe owner trying to scale up, so the client attends to the logic rather than immediately analysing their own business.

Give them a taste with an entry-level teaser model: a break-even model for a product or sales business (how many extra cups of coffee justify hiring the new staff member), or a wages model for an hours-based business (how fast profit is lost to downtime, sick leave and unbillable hours).
Listen for the buying signal — "yes, that's really useful", "oh, that's kind of intriguing" — before going any further.

Then briefly flash a fully built, complex industry model, still in an unrelated industry and strictly high level: enough to show what happens when marketing costs, customer types and peak periods all pull together in one dynamic space.
Ask whether they see value in a bespoke model built for their own strategic planning, hiring decisions or equipment purchases.

When they say yes, enforce a gap of time before they see their own model. The pause is what lets mental ownership form — a client has to want what the model does before they will spend the energy needed to understand their own data.

materials.name: Trial Fit Method
materials.summary: A staged way of putting a real model in front of a motivated client, built on the tailored suit metaphor: this is an off-the-rack model that gets fitted over time, not a bespoke build. Working in best guesses rather than waiting for perfect data keeps the session moving — get it down, then get it good. The moment that changes the client is comparing their own guesses against their actual financial performance.
materials.who_when: Clients who already have awareness or motivation — the bank wants a cash forecast, they want to test the feasibility of an idea, they are mid strategic plan, or they rang after the introductory video or quiz.
steps: Prime the client before the meeting where you can; an introductory video does the framing work in advance.

Frame the session with the tailored suit metaphor: an off-the-rack model saves the time and money of weaving the fabric yourself, and like any suit it needs fittings. That creates permission for it to be imperfect at first.
Give a quick global overview — what the pages are and what each does, whether that is job types, revenue, seasonal wages or material calculations — without lingering on the detail.
Get them in the water: drop straight down to a page or cell you picked in advance and ask for their best guess on a metric.
Use outlandish numbers deliberately at this stage — a whole residential build at $263,000 — so the client learns how the model behaves without the burden of finding real data.
Do not reach for their actual data yet; finding and entering it themselves is how they take ownership of the model.
Then test the guesses against actual financial performance. A large gap says the everyday assumptions behind their quoting, hiring and purchasing decisions are disconnected from reality.
Run scenarios off that gap — move productive time from 85% to 92% and show the exact threshold required just to break even.
Where the required rate is unrealistic — expecting 7.5 billable hours out of an 8-hour day — the data-backed decision is to raise charge-out rates rather than demand an impossible standard.
Set homework: have them play with the model and answer four questions — what can they measure, what matters most, how would knowing it change a decision, and is it actually actionable.
Reconvene on their answers, and use them to guide the final tailoring and the integration with forecasting and planning.

advisor_guidance.sequencing_cautious_vs_trial: Cautious Reveal is for low-awareness clients who need to be sold on the idea first. Trial Fit is for already-motivated clients who just need to be introduced to the model. They are designed to work in sequence for low-awareness clients: Cautious Reveal in meeting one, Trial Fit in meeting two.
advisor_guidance.feasibility_vs_modelling: Use the Lite Feasibility Framework when a client wants to acquire something specific (asset, loan, new initiative). Use revenue modelling tools when the client wants to understand and improve ongoing profitability. The Lite Feasibility assessment often leads naturally into a revenue model conversation once the payback case is established.
advisor_guidance.profit_squeeze_entry_point: When a client presents with rising costs, margin pressure, or cost squeeze, the primary goal is to quantify the gap between current and target performance. Revenue models make this gap visible and actionable. Introduce the Why Use Revenue Models rationale first to build advisor confidence and client buy-in before opening any model.
